newsitem.title: FRANCE: INSTANT VIEW - Bank of France nominations.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Bank of France nominations.

text.p: Following is a selection of reactions to the nomination of Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard to the Bank of France's monetary policy council.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said earlier Guillen and Bernard would replace Jean Boissonnat and Bruno de Maulde, whose mandates expire next week. Prime Minister Alain Juppe said the appointments did not imply any change in policy direction.
SONJA GIBBS, BOND STRATEGIST, NOMURA INTERNATIONAL
"The fact that the franc is slightly weaker suggests that there is concern that the weight of opinion could shift slightly on the council."
The market is pricing in rate cuts in the first quarter of 1997; I don't think the appointments change that. Even though Boissonnat is gone I don't see any real change coming here."

"The first point is that I don't think it will change the broad lines of exchange rate policy. The French franc will remain pegged to the deutsche mark within the former bands of the ERM (exchange rate mechanism).
They will stick to the former ERM bands but I'm not sure they will continue to target 3.35."

"The Bank of France is likely to cut rates faster than before, at least until the German repo (rate) level is reached. Whether the Bank of France could try to cut rates below the German level is now an open question whereas before it was not.
"I think there's a 40 percent chance, and in my view it would be negative for French markets, it would weaken the currency and the bond market."
"These are people not too firmly in the Trichet camp. At least I would say that about Guillen and we suspect Bernard of not being a Maastrichtien of the first order.

"This is rather a surprise. I was expecting Boissonnat to be renominated. These nominations reinforce diversity on the monetary policy council. Either opposition to Trichet is being created which could lead to more openness to lower rates, and I think Anglo Saxons will move rapidly toward this interpretation.
Another reading is that we're getting people with a different view, who may think differently. It could be rather a good thing that we don't have a whole council of people who think alike."

(The nominations) will reinforce the debate on the status of the euro. Should we have a single currency that serves trade and growth or should we continue to follow traditional medium-term targets and aim for the strongest possible currency?"
JEAN-LOUIS MOURIER, ECONOMIST, LOUIS DREYFUS FINANCE

"There will be no change of monetary policy. There will perhaps be more internal debate. I don't think they will cut the intervention rate to three percent next Thursday. It's a signal to Trichet: putting in people who won't follow him blindly, even if there is no change in monetary policy.
